title: How2To
description: UI design and UX research for How2To, step-by-step spatial tutorials for Vision Pro, Meta Quest and iOS, designed over four months at Omnia.
hmw: transform static digital tutorials into interactive, spatial experiences that are easier to follow, retain, and apply, especially for complex tasks like tech repairs or cooking?

blocks.text: Tutorials on a flat screen make people stop and switch between the content and the task. Over four months at Omnia, I was UI designer and UX researcher on How2To: step-by-step tutorials that sit in the room with you on Vision Pro, Meta Quest and iOS.

items.title: Brainstorming Sessions

source.text: Held 5 internal sessions to ideate onboarding flows, spatial interactions, and modular templates (e.g., stove/oven marker for cooking, screw guide for repair).

items.condensed: I held five internal sessions to ideate onboarding flows, spatial interactions, and modular templates like stove markers and screw guides.

items.title: Competitor Analysis

source.text: Analyzed spatial learning and tutorial platforms (e.g., JigSpace, WikiHow VR, YouTube with AR extensions).
Identified gaps in interactive guidance, spatial UX fidelity, and lack of cross-context template systems for different task types (DIY, cooking, tech repair).

items.condensed: I analyzed platforms like JigSpace and WikiHow VR, finding gaps in interactive guidance, spatial fidelity, and cross-context templates.

items.title: User Interviews

source.text: Interviewed 9 participants (ages 20–45) who regularly engage with instructional content online (YouTube, blogs, mobile apps).

items: 7/9 struggle to pause / switch between content and task
6/9 expressed interest in hands-free visual instruction
5/9 found current AR tools either non-intuitive or overly complex

items.condensed: I interviewed nine people aged 20 to 45: seven struggled to switch between content and task, and six wanted hands-free visual instruction.

items.title: Persona Building

items: DIY Dan: 32, uses YouTube for repairs, needs visual clarity
Chef Lila: 28, uses Instagram Reels for recipes, wants step control
Tinker Tim: 24, builds PCs, frustrated with switching apps during work

items.condensed: I built three user personas from interview data: a DIY repairer, a home cook, and a computer builder.

items.title: Affinity Mapping

items: Friction in switching between instruction and action
Demand for real-time, spatial, context-aware tutorials
Excitement around using headsets for hands-free guidance

items.condensed: I clustered interview responses around multitasking load, switching friction, demand for spatial tutorials, and headset interest for hands-free guidance.

blocks.text: Voice that stays out of the way

I designed a voice-first interaction model that avoids cognitive overload by keeping only the most contextually relevant commands. On Vision Pro, the voice layer acts as a spatial tutorial assistant: it generates steps enriched with task-specific videos and images, so users can focus on the hands-on activity. The design follows minimalism and keeps the flow continuous in 3D space.

Once the AI generates a tutorial, this page lets the user review the results, sources and ingredients, and check they have the right tools before starting.
If they don’t approve, they can open “Browse” or “See More”, or use voice search to regenerate with a new prompt. “Continue” opens the immersive viewer.

I designed two viewer sizes. The immersive view keeps users focused on a single task. The condensed view shows more information and leaves room for other apps. In user testing, we found people used to spatial interfaces keep 3-4 applications in view, and the condensed view suits them. It is also in demand in B2B settings, where worker efficiency matters more than immersion.
I organized generated tutorials into easy-to-navigate sections such as “Food”, “DIY” and “Technology”, using distinct, colorful cards so each tutorial is easy to find and pleasant to browse.

How2To does more than the native media controls allow, so I redesigned them. From left to right: Steps, access to tutorials, a toggle for the viewer mode, show or hide ingredients, and information sources.

The controls keep a small footprint, so they save space without losing functionality.

cards.label: Fewer voice commands
cards.value: Chose a voice model that keeps only the most contextually relevant commands, because it avoids cognitive overload during hands-on work.

cards.label: Two viewer sizes
cards.value: Chose an immersive and a condensed viewer over one size, because focused tasks need immersion, while people running 3-4 apps and B2B workers need room for more.

cards.label: Custom media controls
cards.value: Chose redesigned controls over the native ones, because How2To needed Steps, viewer mode, ingredients and sources in a small footprint.

blocks.text: What this study can and can’t show

items: The research is nine interviews. The 7 of 9, 6 of 9 and 5 of 9 counts are directional, not statistics.
I have no outcome metrics for How2To, such as task completion or time on task. What I can show is the design and the research behind it.
